\\n <p>En 1950, le cartographe su:
In 1950, the Swiss cartographer Eduard Imhof published tables of walking speed measured on mountain trails, by slope. In 1993, the geographer Waldo Tobler looked for a simple formula fitting these measurements. He chose an exponential of the slope:

v = 6 · e−3.5 · |s + 0.05| km/h, where s is the slope (0.10 for +10%)

The 6 is the maximum speed; the +0.05 puts that maximum on a gentle descent (−5%); the 3.5 sets how fast you slow down as the slope moves away from −5%, in either direction. On the flat: 5.0 km/h; at +20%: 2.5 km/h.

\\n <p>En 1908, <b>William Gosset:
In 1908, William Gosset, a chemist at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, was checking the quality of barley on small samples. He noticed that when the mean and standard deviation are estimated from few measurements, extreme deviations come up more often than the normal distribution predicts. As Guinness forbade publishing under his own name, he signed “Student”.

The construction. Take a normal variable Z and divide it by a noisy estimate of its standard deviation, built from ν other normal variables (a χ² distribution with ν degrees of freedom):

T = Z / √(χ²ν / ν) → density ∝ (1 + t²/ν)−(ν+1)/2

When the denominator happens to be small, T becomes large: that is what thickens the tails. The larger ν, the more stable the estimate of the standard deviation, and the more T looks like Z. At ν = 1 it is the Cauchy distribution, with extreme tails; as ν goes to infinity, it is exactly the normal distribution.

Here it is used as a model with three settings: a centre, a width, and ν. Fitted on my

This heart rate variability (HRV) is driven by the nervous system: rested, it lets the heart vary a lot; tired or stressed, it tightens it. D’où vient la simulation de Monte Carlo: Where Monte Carlo simulation comes from
\\n <p><b>L’origine.</b> En 1946, à:
The origin. In 1946, at Los Alamos, the mathematician Stanislaw Ulam, convalescing, wondered what the chance of winning a game of solitaire was. The exact calculation was impossible; he had the idea of playing the game hundreds of times and counting the wins. With John von Neumann, he applied the idea to the path of neutrons, on the first computers. The code name came from the Monte Carlo casino, where Ulam’s uncle used to gamble.

The principle. When a result depends on many small chances that add up, it is not calculated: it is replayed thousands of times, and the spread of the results is examined.

D’où vient le test de résistance: Where the stress test comes from
\\n <p><b>Le problème.</b> Un modèl:
The problem. A model fitted on the past only knows what it has seen. In 1998, the fund LTCM, run by two Nobel laureates, collapsed: its models, fitted on calm years, judged the Russian crisis almost impossible. In 2008, banks’ VaRs, fitted on 2004–2006, were exceeded day after day.

The answer. Complement the model with imposed scenarios, often historical (“what if 2008 happened again?”): the question is no longer “what is the probability?”, but “if it happens, how much does it cost, and can it be absorbed?”. Since 2009, the Federal Reserve and then the European Banking Authority have imposed these tests on large banks.

The idea. In 1966, Ronald Howard founded decision analysis on one rule: a decision is judged on what was known when it was made, not on what happened.
